title: Llamadas: phone calls
_note: business-spanish run, 2026-11-07: written by hand for Spain, not yet read by a human. Phone numbers in the models are invented. Words already in the lexicon or another deck are refs; deHint = German translation (the 'German' tab).
intro: On the phone you can't point, smile or look anything up, so a few fixed phrases do most of the work. This unit follows a call from start to finish: answering, saying who you are, asking for someone, leaving a message and asking the other person to repeat. Use usted with clients and offices until they offer tú. With colleagues, tú is normal.
introEasy: Are you afraid of phone calls in Spanish? Learn the short phrases that help you start, ask and finish a call.

phrases.en: Hello? (answering the phone)

es419.note: Latin America varies: ¿Aló? in much of South America, ¿Bueno? in Mexico.

phrases.en: Hello? (answering your own mobile)

phrases.use: Saying who you are and why
phrases.en: Is this a good moment?

es419.note: Pillar in this sense is Spain. Latin America: ¿Es buen momento?

phrases.es: ¿Podría hablar con la señora Gil, por favor?
phrases.en: Could I speak to Ms Gil, please?
Is Marta there, please?
Could you put me through to accounts, please?

es419.note: Latin America often says comunicar con instead of pasar con.

phrases.en: Who's calling, please?

phrases.es: Un momento, por favor. Le paso.
phrases.en: One moment, please. I'll put you through.
Please hold.
The line is busy.

es419.note: Comunicando is Spain. Latin America says the line is ocupada.

phrases.en: She's in a meeting right now.
Would you like to leave a message for her/him?

es419.note: Latin America more often says un mensaje.

phrases.es: ¿Puede decirle que me llame, por favor?
phrases.en: Could you ask her/him to call me, please?

phrases.es: Le doy mi número. ¿Tiene para apuntar?
phrases.en: I'll give you my number. Do you have something to write with?

phrases.es: Se lo digo en cuanto termine.
phrases.en: I'll tell her/him as soon as she/he finishes.
Sorry, I can't hear you very well.
Could you repeat that more slowly, please?
Could you spell that for me?
Sorry, you keep breaking up.

phrases.es: Creo que se ha equivocado de número.
phrases.en: I think you have the wrong number.

phrases.es: Entonces le envío el presupuesto hoy mismo.
phrases.en: So I'll send you the quote later today.

phrases.es: Muchas gracias por llamar. Un saludo.
phrases.en: Thank you for calling. Goodbye.
OK, thanks. Bye.

es419.note: Venga as OK is Spain. Latin America uses bueno or dale, depending on the country.

models.title: A caller leaves a message
models.text:
—Reformas Ibáñez, buenos días. Le atiende Lucía. ¿En qué puedo ayudarle?
—Buenos días. Soy Adil Benali, de Transportes Sur. ¿Podría hablar con el señor Romero?
—Un momento, por favor. No se retire.
—Gracias.
—¿Señor Benali? Lo siento, ahora mismo está reunido. ¿Quiere dejarle algún recado?
—Sí, por favor. Llamaba por la entrega del jueves. Tenemos que pasarla al viernes por la mañana.
—De acuerdo. Perdone, ¿me puede deletrear el apellido?
—Claro. Be de Barcelona, e, ene, a, ele, i.
—Muy bien. ¿Y un teléfono de contacto?
—Sí, el 555 40 77 19.
—Perfecto. Se lo digo en cuanto termine.
—Muchas gracias. Un saludo.
—Gracias a usted. Hasta luego.
notes: Spanish marks each new speaker with a long dash (—) and no quotation marks.
Llamaba por… (I was calling about…) uses the imperfect to sound polite, not to talk about the past.
In cuanto (as soon as) takes the subjunctive when the action is still to come: en cuanto termine.
Spelling aloud: people give a place or a name for the letters that sound alike, as in be de Barcelona. Name the letter first, then the word.
Read the number in groups, as it is written here: quinientos cincuenta y cinco, cuarenta, setenta y siete, diecinueve.

models.title: Two colleagues on a bad line
models.text:
—¿Sí?
—Hola, Marta, soy Javi. ¿Te pillo bien?
—Sí, dime.
—Oye, ¿tienes el número del proveedor de Sevilla?
—Perdona, es que se corta. Estoy en el tren. ¿Qué decías?
—Que si tienes el número del proveedor de Sevilla.
—Ah, sí. Te lo mando por WhatsApp, ¿vale?
—Perfecto. Venga, gracias. Hasta luego.
—Hasta luego.
notes: Dime (tell me) is how you invite someone to talk. With a client: dígame.
Que si… is how you repeat a question when the other person didn't hear it. A statement repeats with que alone: Que mañana no vengo.
Spanish phone calls often end fast, with several short words: venga, gracias, hasta luego. It isn't rude.

tips: Prepare your first sentence before you dial: who you are and why you are calling. Soy…, de… Le llamo por… Everything after that is easier.
Tell people early that Spanish isn't your first language: Perdone, hablo un poco despacio. Most people then slow down too.
Have a pen ready. Numbers and dates are what you most need to get right, so read them back to check: El 555 40 77 19, ¿verdad?
Spaniards often read a phone number in groups of two or three, not digit by digit. If that is too fast, ask: ¿Me lo puede decir cifra por cifra?

exercises.context: You answer the phone in an office in Spain.
exercises.explain: ¿Dígame? (literally: tell me) is the usual way to answer in Spain.

es419.note: Spain's way of answering. Latin America varies by country.

exercises.prompt: Le llamo ___ la factura de marzo.
exercises.explain: Llamar por + noun gives the reason for the call. Para goes with a verb: le llamo para confirmar.

exercises.prompt: Llamaba ___ confirmar la cita del lunes.
exercises.explain: Para + infinitive gives the purpose of the call. Compare: por + noun, para + verb.

exercises.context: You answer and want to know who is calling.
exercises.explain: ¿De parte de quién? is the fixed phrase: who's calling?

exercises.prompt: Un momento, por favor. Le ___ con la señora Gil.
exercises.explain: Pasar con is to put someone through to a person: le paso con…

exercises.context: To a client: asking them to hold.
exercises.explain: A negative command with usted takes the subjunctive form: no se retire.

exercises.context: You called, and the line is busy.
exercises.prompt: He llamado dos veces, pero está ___.
exercises.explain: In Spain a busy line está comunicando.
Un recado is a short message for someone. Un pedido is an order.

exercises.context: You didn't catch how a name is written.
exercises.explain: Deletrear is to spell out, letter by letter.

exercises.prompt: Creo que se ha ___ de número.
exercises.explain: Equivocarse de + noun means to get the wrong one: equivocarse de número, de día, de puerta.
En cuanto takes the subjunctive when the action hasn't happened yet.

exercises.context: You call a colleague and check it is a good moment.
exercises.explain: ¿Te pillo bien? (literally: do I catch you well?) is everyday Spanish in Spain. With a client: ¿Le viene bien ahora?

es419.note: Pillar in this sense is Spain only.
